lead: Most diffusion problems assume a tube of fixed cross-section. In real equipment the path often widens or narrows: vapour leaves a droplet, gas enters a spherical pellet, liquid falls down a tube. The total molar flow W stays the same through every slice, but the flux changes because the area A(z) changes. Fick's law is therefore written with A(z) inside and integrated over the geometry. When a boundary such as a subliming surface moves slowly, each instant can be treated as steady; this pseudo-steady result sizes evaporating droplets and the Stefan tube.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.4 for the stagnant-film flux, and the integration of 1/A.

sections.h3: Total rate is constant, flux is not

blocks.text: Pick a coordinate z along the diffusion path. Let W be the total molar flow of A in mol/s. In steady state W is the same through every cross-section: nothing accumulates. The area A(z) in m² changes with z, so the flux N<sub>A</sub> = W/A(z) in mol/(m²·s) changes too. Fick's law applies at each slice, not to the whole shape at once.

blocks.where: W is total molar flow of A (mol/s); A(z) is cross-sectional area (m²); N<sub>A</sub> is molar flux of A (mol/(m²·s)); D is diffusivity (m²/s); c<sub>A</sub> is concentration of A (mol/m³); z is distance along the path (m). This form is for equimolar diffusion or a dilute A.

blocks.text: Rearrange and integrate between two stations 1 and 2: W∫dz/A = −D∫dc<sub>A</sub>. The left side depends only on geometry; the right side only on concentrations. For a constant-area tube A cancels, and you recover Chapter 1.4. For a varying area, carry A(z) inside the integral.

For diffusion of A through stagnant B, replace the concentration gradient term by c dy<sub>A</sub>/(1−y<sub>A</sub>), where c is total concentration (mol/m³) and y<sub>A</sub> is mole fraction of A. The same integration then produces a logarithm, as the sphere below shows.

For a sphere of radius R losing A into a stagnant gas, A(r)=4πr². At distance r from the centre, W = −D(4πr²)c/(1−y<sub>A</sub>) dy<sub>A</sub>/dr. Separate variables and integrate from the surface (r=R, y<sub>A</sub>=y<sub>As</sub>) to the bulk (r→∞, y<sub>A</sub>=0).

blocks.where: W is molar flow of A leaving the sphere (mol/s); R is sphere radius (m); D is diffusivity of A in the gas (m²/s); c is total concentration (mol/m³); y<sub>As</sub> is mole fraction of A at the surface.

blocks.text: If both sides are equimolar and the two spheres have radii R₁ and R₂, the same integration gives W = 4πD(c<sub>A1</sub> − c<sub>A2</sub>)/(1/R₁ − 1/R₂). Here c<sub>A1</sub> and c<sub>A2</sub> are the concentrations of A at the two surfaces in mol/m³. The denominator is positive when R₁ < R₂.
A cylinder uses A=2πrL, so ∫dr/r gives ln(r₂/r₁). A cone uses A=πr(z)² with r(z) linear in z, giving a rational integral. The recipe never changes: write A(z), separate, integrate.

sections.h3: Pseudo-steady state: a boundary that moves

blocks.text: A subliming ball or an evaporating droplet has a surface that moves. The gas film around it holds very little material compared with the amount that crosses during the process. The concentration profile therefore adjusts in seconds, while the radius changes over hours. At any instant the steady formula applies with the current radius. This is the pseudo-steady-state assumption.

For a ball, the moles left in the solid are N = (4/3)πR³ρ/M, where ρ is solid density (kg/m³) and M is molar mass (kg/mol). Differentiating, dN/dt = 4πR²(ρ/M)dR/dt. This loss equals −W. Using the stagnant-sphere W gives R dR/dt = −D c L M/ρ, with L = ln(1/(1−y<sub>As</sub>)). Integrate from R₁ at t=0 to R at t: R₁² − R² = 2(D c L M/ρ)t. The time depends on R₁² − R², not on R₁ − R.

The falling liquid level in a narrow tube is the same balance. With the gas path z above the liquid, ρ<sub>L</sub>/M · dz/dt = N<sub>A</sub> = D c (y<sub>A1</sub> − y<sub>A2</sub>)/[z (y<sub>B</sub>)<sub>lm</sub>], so the level falls from z₀ to z in a time t = ρ<sub>L</sub> (y<sub>B</sub>)<sub>lm</sub> (z² − z₀²)/[2 M D c (y<sub>A1</sub> − y<sub>A2</sub>)]. This is the Stefan tube, and read backwards it measures D (Winkelmann's method, in the next chapter). The pseudo-steady assumption fails at very short times, when the profile has not yet formed; during fast changes of temperature or pressure; and when the vapour is not dilute compared with the condensed phase, for example a volatile liquid close to its boiling point, because the gas then stores a large share of the material that crosses.

figure.caption: The mothball of the worked example: its radius follows R² = R₁² − 2kt, so it shrinks slowly at first and fast at the end. It halves to 5 mm after 143 days and would vanish after about 190 days, because the vapour pressure at the surface is only 11 Pa.

examples.question: A naphthalene ball (a mothball) of radius 10 mm sublimes in still air at 298 K and 1 atm. Take D = 6.1×10⁻⁶ m²/s for naphthalene in air, a vapour pressure of 11 Pa at the surface (about 0.08 mmHg), and zero naphthalene far away. M = 128 g/mol and the solid density is ρ = 1140 kg/m³. Find the time for the radius to fall to 5 mm, assuming pseudo-steady diffusion.
steps: Data in SI: R₁ = 0.010 m, R₂ = 0.005 m, M = 0.128 kg/mol. Total concentration c = P/(RT) = 101325/(8.314 × 298) = 40.9 mol/m³.
Surface mole fraction: y<sub>As</sub> = 11/101325 = 1.086×10⁻⁴. The log factor ln(1/(1 − y<sub>As</sub>)) = 1.086×10⁻⁴; at this dilution it equals y<sub>As</sub>.
Rate from the ball at radius R: W = 4πR D c ln(1/(1 − y<sub>As</sub>)) = 4πR (6.1×10⁻⁶)(40.9)(1.086×10⁻⁴) = 3.40×10⁻⁷ R mol/s. At R = 10 mm, W = 3.40×10⁻⁹ mol/s, about 0.038 g per day.
Moles in the solid: N = (4/3)πR³ρ/M, so dN/dt = 4πR²(ρ/M) dR/dt. The mass balance dN/dt = −W gives 4πR²(ρ/M) dR/dt = −4πR D c ln(1/(1 − y<sub>As</sub>)).
Integrate R dR = −k dt from R₁ to R₂: t = (R₁² − R₂²)/(2k) = (1.0×10⁻⁴ − 2.5×10⁻⁵)/(2 × 3.04×10⁻¹²) = 1.23×10⁷ s.
examples.answer: About 1.23×10⁷ s, roughly 143 days (nearly five months), for the radius to halve. The tiny vapour pressure, not D, makes a mothball last a season. Air movement in a real cupboard adds convection and shortens this time.

traps: Using a fixed area and forgetting A(z): W is constant through the shape, but flux N<sub>A</sub> = W/A(z) is not.
For stagnant B, using the plain dc<sub>A</sub>/dz form and missing the 1/(1−y<sub>A</sub>) factor; this loses the logarithm ln(1/(1−y<sub>As</sub>)).
Integrating the sphere as if R were the variable instead of R²; the time contains R₁² − R₂², not R₁ − R₂.
A sign slip: W is positive outward, but dR/dt is negative for a shrinking ball. Keep the loss as −W.
Applying pseudo-steady state at very short times or when the gas dissolves appreciably, where the gas holdup is not small.

quiz.q: In steady diffusion through a variable cross-section, which quantity is constant through every slice: total molar flow W or flux N<sub>A</sub>?
quiz.a: W is constant. The flux N<sub>A</sub> = W/A(z) changes because the area changes.

quiz.q: Why does the stagnant-sphere rate contain ln(1/(1−y<sub>As</sub>)) while equimolar diffusion between two spheres contains a plain concentration difference?
quiz.a: In stagnant B, A must drift through B, so the flux carries the factor 1/(1−y<sub>A</sub>). Integrating this factor gives the logarithm. For equimolar counter-diffusion the bulk terms cancel, leaving the plain difference.

quiz.q: A sphere of radius 2 mm loses A into stagnant gas. D = 1.0×10⁻⁵ m²/s, c = 40 mol/m³, y<sub>As</sub> = 0.0200. Find W.
In the pseudo-steady model a naphthalene ball falls from 10 mm to 5 mm in a time t. If the initial radius were 20 mm, would it fall to 10 mm in the same time t? Explain.
quiz.a: No. R² = R₁² − 2kt, and the worked case gives 2kt = 10² − 5² = 75 mm². Starting at 20 mm, after the same t, R² = 400 − 75 = 325 mm², so R = 18.0 mm. The radius drops only 2 mm, because the time depends on R₁² − R², not on R₁ − R: a bigger ball loses more moles per mm of radius.

quiz.q: In a Stefan tube, the liquid level falls slowly while diffusion occurs above it. Why can the diffusion be treated as steady at each instant?
quiz.a: The gas column holds very little solute compared with the amount crossing, so the concentration profile adjusts almost instantly. The level moves slowly, so the steady formula applies with the current column length.

quiz.q: Equimolar diffusion occurs between two spheres of radii 5 mm and 15 mm. D = 2.0×10⁻⁵ m²/s, c<sub>A1</sub> = 0.5 mol/m³, c<sub>A2</sub> = 0.1 mol/m³. Find W.
Give two situations where the pseudo-steady assumption fails for an evaporating droplet, and explain what is wrong in each.
quiz.a: First, at very short times the concentration profile around a fresh droplet has not formed yet: the true early rate is higher than the steady value and changes with time, so the steady formula is wrong until the profile settles. Second, for a volatile liquid close to its boiling point y<sub>As</sub> approaches 1: the vapour is no longer dilute compared with the liquid, the gas stores a large share of what evaporates and the surface moves fast, so each instant is not steady. Fast temperature or pressure changes break the assumption in the same way.

beyond: Not for the exam. The same moving-boundary integral describes shrinking aerosol droplets, burning carbon particles, and drug release from a slowly dissolving pellet. Research checks the pseudo-steady result against the full diffusion equation with a moving boundary, often solved numerically. Freeze-drying and the sublimation purification of solids use the same balance. Search next for the Stefan tube, moving-boundary diffusion, and the shrinking-core model.
